senses: Having multiple paths, channels or configurations
Resembling lichen
Gin produced in Schiedam, a southern municipality of the Netherlands.
To take on; undertake; assume.
ety: From Middle English ontaken, equivalent to on- + take. Compare Old English onniman (“to receive, take”).

senses: A container of Asian derivation, usually handleless, used to hold liquid with a broad opening on top for inserting liquid and usually only one spout for pouring.
ety: Borrowed from Malay kendi, from Sanskrit कुण्ड (kuṇḍa) or कुण्डिक (kuṇḍika, “water pot”).

senses: The end of a sari that hangs loose over the shoulder.
ety: Borrowed from Hindi आँचल (ā̃cal), from Sanskrit अञ्चल (añcala).

senses: A kind of whitish-grey fur from the winter coat of the least weasel.
ety: From Middle English letuse, from Anglo-Norman letuse; further etymology is unknown.

senses: A depiction of a bird similar to a house martin or swallow with stylized feet.
ety: From Middle English martilet, probably a blend of martinet (“martin”; from Middle French martinet and Medieval Latin martineta) and Middle French merlet.

senses: The process of making stereotype plates and printing from them.
ety: Borrowed from French stéréotypie, from stéréotype + -ie. By surface analysis, stereotype + -y (suffix forming abstract nouns).

senses: The fourth generation or great-grandchildren of Japanese immigrants, particularly in North America and in Latin America.
ety: From Japanese 四世 (よんせい (yonsei)), from 四 (yon-, “fourth”) + 世 (sei, “generation”).

senses: A woven Maori cloak covered with muka tassels.
A type of cartridge used in some handguns.
A type of German semiautomatic pistol.
ety: For Latin parā bellum (“furnish war”), from the Latin adage sī vīs pācem, parā bellum (“if you want peace, prepare for war”).

senses: The American elk (Cervus canadensis).
Having biological, psychological and social characteristics.
One trillion (10¹², or 1,000,000,000,000) bytes or 1,000 gigabytes.
Familiar term of address for a boy; bub; bubba.
ety: Perhaps from brother, as pronounced by young children who are not yet able to properly pronounce its complex consonants, but alternatively perhaps from Pennsylvania German; see bub. Compare sissy.
examples: Mother sent me to hunt you; she is dying, and sissy and bubby are hungry and the baby is crying, and we're afraid the cross man will come.

senses: A boot (storage compartment) located at the front rather than the rear of a car, especially an electric vehicle.
The art or composition of poetry.
ety: From Middle English poesie (Middle English po(esie) + -esy), from Middle French poesie, from Late Latin poesia, from earlier poēsis, from Ancient Greek ποίησις (poíēsis). Doublet of poiesis.

senses: The pulverized rhizome of the turmeric plant, used for flavoring and to add a bright yellow color to food.
A yellow to reddish-brown dye extracted from the turmeric plant.
ety: From Middle English turmeryte, tarmaret, of uncertain origin. Possibly corrupted from Arabic كُرْكُم (kurkum, “Curcuma”) or from Old French terre mérite (“deserving earth”), potentially as a folk etymology of the Arabic.

senses: To subject to the nitriding process.
A physical exercise or cosmetic product intended to firm part of the body.
A thin chisel with a tang to enter the handle instead of a socket for receiving it.
That swoops or swoop.
examples: With a huge rush of wind a swooping eagle dropped from out of the night sky.

senses: autobiography
ety: Clipping. By surface analysis, auto- + bio.

senses: An arapaima (Arapaima gigas), a large fish of the Amazon.
geospatial information
A science and technology which develops and uses information science to address problems of geography, geosciences and related branches of engineering
A technique whereby the video output of one source, or a specific reference signal, is used to synchronize other sources.
A banker or moneychanger.
ety: Borrowed from Persian صراف (sarâf) or Urdu صراف (sarrāf), from Arabic صَرَّاف (ṣarrāf).

senses: Not perishable; not subject to decay; enduring permanently.
ety: From Middle French impérissable. See im- + perishable.
examples: The child was to be a prophet, unrivalled among men, and the parent of an imperishable race.

senses: A kind of Asian horoscope.
An inevitable condition or outcome.
Of an element: lying beyond uranium in the periodic table; having an atomic number greater than 92.
To shout yee-haw, or exclaim in a similar manner.
ety: From gee and haw, words used to instruct a horse to turn in different directions.

senses: One who studies reptiles and amphibians; a reptile and amphibian specialist.
ety: From herpeto- (From Ancient Greek ἑρπετόν (herpetón, “creeping animal, reptile, especially a snake”)) + -logist.
examples: Already, Griffith has observed several amphibian extinctions. Pretty much every herpetologist working out in the field has watched several.

senses: A member or supporter of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh.
ety: Borrowed from Hindi संघी (saṅghī), from Hindi संघ (saṅgh, “association, union”), clipping of राष्ट्रीय स्वयंसेवक संघ (rāṣṭrīya svayansevak saṅgh, “Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh”), a Hindu nationalist right-wing group in India.
examples: By using Sanghi, Digvijaya Singh is apparently referring to the RSS, the parent organisation of the BJP.

senses: The insertion or intercalation of days into the calendar in order to correct the error arising from the difference between the civil year and the solar year.
An intercalated prayer for deliverance from evil coming after the Lord's Prayer.
The variable body of a liturgical preface, between the protocol and eschatocol, typically stating the motive for worship on a given day.
ety: The term was coined in 1848 by Rudolf Virchow. From Old French embolisme (“intercalation of days in a calendar to correct errors”), from Late Latin embolismus, from Ancient Greek ἐμβολισμός (embolismós, “intercalary”), from ἐμβάλλω (embállō, “to insert, throw in”).

senses: Prepared in an Italian style with wine, mushrooms, spices and tomatoes.
Money, riches, or wealth, especially when seen as having a corrupting effect or causing greed, or obtained in an underhanded manner.
ety: From Middle English lūcre, lucor, lucour, lucur (“gain in money, profit; money; wages; illicit gain; advantage, benefit”), from Old French lucre or Latin lucrum (“advantage, profit; love of gain, avarice”), from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂w- (“gain, profit”) + *-tlom (variant of *-trom (suffix forming nouns denoting tools or instruments)).

senses: Usage of geological techniques in archaeology.
The place in the above-ground part of a coal mine where coal is washed.
Synonym of laundromat, launderette.
